chunks: Standard UART baud rates. The question: What are some standard communication rates?
The standard UART speeds are 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200 baud. Baud is bits per second on the wire.
The two you meet most are 9600, common on GPS modules and old sensors, and 115200, the usual default for debug consoles.
Because each byte needs 10 bits on the wire, the bytes per second are one tenth of the baud rate.
Imagine a master wheel spinning fast, with a chain of gears that slow it down. Each gear divides the speed by a whole number.
The standard UART speeds are exactly what you get from one special master wheel, 1. 8432 megahertz, divided by 16 and then by small whole numbers.
If your master wheel is a different speed, you can only choose whole-number gears, so you land slightly off the target.
Time scales as 1/baud, so every doubling of baud halves the transfer time. A 100 kB firmware image takes about 8.
9 seconds at 115200 baud but 107 seconds at 9600, which is why bootloaders ask for the higher rate when the link allows it.
Baud: symbols per second. For UART each symbol is one bit, so 115200 baud is 115200 bits per second. 8N1: the usual frame: 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, with a start bit.
That is 10 bits per byte. Baud-rate divisor: the number the chip divides its clock by to make the bit timing.
Divider error: how far the achieved rate lands from the target, because the divisor must be a whole number. Crystal: the part that sets the chip's clock frequency.
At 115200 baud one bit lasts 1 over 115200 about 8. 68 microseconds. A 10-bit frame takes about 86. 8 microseconds, so you move about 11,520 bytes per second.
Now take a 16 megahertz clock whose receiver counts 16 ticks per bit. The divisor should be 16 000 000 over (16 times 115200) about 8. 68 , but it must round to 9.
That gives 111,111 baud, about 3. 5% too slow. Using a 14. 7456 megahertz crystal instead gives a whole divisor and zero error. That is the whole idea.
